newsitem.title: USA: GM, union reach deal to settle Ohio strike.
newsitem.headline: GM, union reach deal to settle Ohio strike.

text.p: General Motors Corp. said it reached a tentative agreement early on Wednesday to end a strike at its Warren, Ohio, wiring harness plants, just over 24 hours after the walkout began.

Deborah Ayers, a spokeswoman for GM's Delphi Packard Electric, said the company reached the deal with the International Union of Electronics Workers Local 717 at about 12:45 a.m. EST. She said details of the agreement were not available.
"We hope to get everyone back to work today," Ayers said of the 8,200 hourly workers involved in the strike.
The strike was one of three local walkouts that GM was battling simultaneously and had the potential to cause a broad shutdown of its North American car and truck operations.

Most GM vehicles built in the United States, Canada and Mexico use wiring harness components and other electrical parts made at the Warren plants. The harnesses, assembled largely in Mexico, are used to distribute electrical power and signals throughout cars and trucks.
The Delphi Packard Electric Division supplies parts to 34 other car and truck manufacturers worldwide and a number of them also could have been affected.

Ayers said if the pact was approved by Local 717 members quickly, no disruptions in vehicle production would occur. She added that details on ratification would be available later on Wednesday. The union rejected a previous tentative agreement in March.

Among demands workers had made in the dispute was for GM to agree not to unilaterally move more jobs to Mexico, where the manual labor required in wiring harness asssembly is much cheaper. The union also sought to abolish the lowest tier of a three-tier wage system, which paid newer workers 55 percent of the full top wage.
The strike started just after midnight EDT on Tuesday. The last strike at the Warren, Ohio, facilities occured in 1971 and lasted about 12 hours.

The settlement leaves GM with two ongoing strikes at two assembly plants in Oklahoma City and Pontiac, Mich. Burnham Securities analyst David Healy estimated on Tuesday that those two walkouts thus far have cost the automaker roughly 43,000 vehicles, or $194 million in lost profits. GM continues to lose about 2,300 vehicles a day to the strikes.

The Oklahoma City plant, idled since April 4, builds GM's new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass cars, while Pontiac, which was struck on April 22, is one of three GM plants that build full-size Chevrolet and GMC pickup trucks.
